citations.quote: Let $M=S^3\times[0,1]$ carry its standard smooth structure. Suppose $f:[0,1]\to M$ is a locally flat proper arc and is a smooth embedding on neighborhoods of its two source endpoints. Then an ambient topological isotopy, equal to the identity on neighborhoods of the two boundary levels of $M$, carries $f$ to a smooth parametrized embedding. It can preserve any smaller prescribed source end collars pointwise.

Let $\alpha:[0,1]\to S^3\times[0,1]$ be a smooth proper embedding with endpoints $(p,0),(p,1)$, whose image agrees with the vertical arc on endpoint product collars. There is a smooth ambient isotopy, fixed near the two boundary levels, taking its image to $\{p\}\times[0,1]$. If $\alpha(s)=(p,s)$ near the source endpoints, the isotopy can take $\alpha(s)$ to $(p,s)$ for every $s$.

derivations.claim: In those collars the image of $\alpha$ is vertical, so write $\alpha(t)=(p,h_0(t))$ near zero and $\alpha(t)=(p,h_1(t))$ near one. Each $h_i$ is an increasing homeomorphism onto its height interval: it is continuous and injective, and the endpoint heights fix its orientation. Choose an increasing homeomorphism $\theta:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ agreeing with the two inverse height functions near the endpoints and interpolate monotonically between them on the remaining middle interval. Then $\beta(s)=\alpha(\theta(s))$ has the same image as $\alpha$ and satisfies $\beta(s)=(p,s)$ on neighborhoods of the source endpoints. In the additional parametrized case take $\theta=\operatorname{id}$. This changes only the parameter used to describe the input image.

Apply [F1] to $\beta$, obtaining an ambient topological isotopy $A_t$ whose final arc $\gamma(s)=A_1(\beta(s))$ is smoothly embedded. Since $A_t$ is fixed near the boundary levels, $\gamma(s)=(p,s)$ near its endpoints. Apply the parametrized clause of [F2] to $\gamma$, obtaining an ambient smooth isotopy $B_t$ fixed near the boundary levels and satisfying $B_1(\gamma(s))=(p,s)$ for every $s$.

Concatenate $A_{2t}$ for $0\le t\le1/2$ with $B_{2t-1}A_1$ for $1/2\le t\le1$. They agree at the joining time. This is a continuous ambient family of homeomorphisms starting at the identity, fixed on a common neighborhood of the two boundary levels. Its terminal map sends the image of $\beta$, and hence the image of $\alpha$, to $\{p\}\times[0,1]$. In the additional parametrized case $\theta=\operatorname{id}$, so it sends $\alpha(s)$ to $(p,s)$ for every $s$. This proves both conclusions without an added choice hypothesis.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Fix the orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ chosen for the mirror convention in the oriented connected-sum definition. If $K$ is a smooth oriented knot, its mirror $r(K)$ carries the orientation induced from $K$ by $r$. The reverse mirror of $K$, denoted $K^\dagger$, is the image $r(K)$ with its knot orientation reversed. Thus $K^\dagger$ changes both the ambient orientation convention and the orientation of the knot.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth.

- The function $f$ is a **Morse function** when every critical point of $f$ is
  nondegenerate
  ([[def-critical-point-and-critical-value-of-a-smooth-function]],
  [[def-nondegenerate-critical-point-nullity-index-and-coindex]]).
- The function $f$ is an **excellent Morse function** when it is Morse and any
  two distinct critical points have distinct critical values.

Thus excellence is stronger than the Morse condition: it excludes repeated
critical values, not repeated indices.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and let $p$ be a critical point of $f$. The
Hessian $\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)$ is a symmetric bilinear form on the
finite-dimensional real vector space $T_pM$
([[def-hessian-of-a-function-at-a-critical-point]]).

- The **nullity** of $p$ for $f$ is
  $$\operatorname{null}_p(f):=\dim\ker\bigl(\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)\bigr).$$
- The critical point $p$ is **nondegenerate** when
  $\operatorname{null}_p(f)=0$.
- The **index** of $p$ for $f$ is the largest dimension of a subspace of $T_pM$
  on which $\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)$ is negative definite.
- The **coindex** of $p$ for $f$ is the largest dimension of a subspace of
  $T_pM$ on which $\operatorname{Hess}_p(f)$ is positive definite.

The positivity and negativity conventions are those of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Cut a short trivial arc from $K$ inside a small ball. Identify its complementary ball with the unit ball $B^3\subset\mathbb R^3$ so that the remaining arc is a smooth embedding $a:[0,1]\to B^3$, its endpoints lie on $S^2$, and its interior lies in the open ball. Straighten its endpoint collars to be radial and transverse to $S^2$. A small perturbation supported away from the endpoints makes $a$ avoid the origin; compactness and the fact that a one-dimensional embedded arc has empty interior allow the perturbation to be chosen arbitrarily small in $C^1$, so it remains embedded and fixed on the endpoint collars. Put $f(s)=\lVert a(s)\rVert^2$. Then $f>0$ on $[0,1]$, $f(0)=f(1)=1$, $f<1$ on $(0,1)$, and transversality gives $f'(0)<0<f'(1)$.

The zeros of $f'$ lie in a compact subinterval of $(0,1)$ because $f'$ is nonzero on the endpoint collars. Cover the zero set by finitely many intervals carrying smooth functions $\phi_i$ supported in $(0,1)$ whose derivatives equal $1$ on smaller intervals still covering the zero set. For $u=(u_i)$ define $f_u=f+\sum_i u_i\phi_i$. On a neighborhood of every zero of $f'$ the total family $\mathcal F(s,u)=f'_u(s)$ is a submersion in the parameter direction, since some $\partial\mathcal F/\partial u_i=\phi_i'(s)=1$. On the compact complement of that neighborhood, $|f'|$ has a positive lower bound, so for all sufficiently small $u$ no new zeros occur there. Thus the total map is transverse to $0$ for parameters in a sufficiently small ball. By [F3], choose a parameter in that ball for which $0$ is a regular value of $f'_u$. The critical points of $f_u$ are then nondegenerate and finite. Shrink the parameter ball so $0<f_u<1$ on the perturbation support. The radial arcs $a_\lambda(s)=\sqrt{f_{\lambda u}(s)/f(s)}\,a(s)$, $0\le\lambda\le1$, form a smooth isotopy of embeddings fixed near the endpoints: the formula is smooth since $f>0$, and sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbations preserve immersion and injectivity on the compact source. By [F4], extend this isotopy in an ambient isotopy supported away from the removed trivial arc, so replacing $a$ by $a_u$ preserves the knot type of its closure. Rename $a_u$ as $a$ and $f_u$ as $f$.

In the unit ball $B^4=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R:\lVert x\rVert^2+t^2\le1\}$ define $\Omega=\{(s,t):0\le s\le1,\ t^2\le1-f(s)\}$ and $D=\{(a(s),t):(s,t)\in\Omega\}$. The map $(s,t)\mapsto(a(s),t)$ is an injective immersion, hence an embedding because $\Omega$ is compact. The function $q(s)=(1-f(s))/(s(1-s))$ extends smoothly and positively to $s=0,1$, with $q(0)=-f'(0)>0$ and $q(1)=f'(1)>0$. Consequently $(s,v)\mapsto(s,v\sqrt{q(s)})$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from the round disk $v^2\le s(1-s)$ onto $\Omega$. The boundary of $\Omega$ is regular: at an interior boundary point $t\ne0$, and at its two endpoints $f'(s)\ne0$, so the differential of $f(s)+t^2$ is nonzero. Thus $D$ is a smooth disk, its boundary lies in $S^3$, and its interior lies in the open four-ball. By [F6], its boundary is exactly the boundary knot specified by properness.

The two boundary arcs of $D$ are the lifts $(a(s),\pm\sqrt{1-f(s)})$ and meet the equatorial $S^2=\{t=0\}\cap S^3$ only at their endpoints. Each hemisphere of $S^3$ is a standard three-ball. Away from a small collar of its equator, projection $(x,t)\mapsto x$ is a smooth diffeomorphism onto the corresponding truncated ball and identifies the lifted arc with $a$. At an endpoint, use the equator collar coordinate $t\ge0$ (or $-t\ge0$ in the lower hemisphere). Since $f'(0)\ne0$ and $f'(1)\ne0$, the implicit function theorem writes the lifted arc near each endpoint as $s=\sigma(t^2)$, with $\sigma$ smooth; in a chart $y$ on the equator its tangential coordinates are $y(t)=y_0+O(t^2)$, while $t$ is the inward collar coordinate. Choose a cutoff $\chi(y,t)$ supported in this chart and equal to $1$ near the arc, and use $(y,t)\mapsto(y-\chi(y,t)(y(t)-y_0),t)$. Its derivative is the identity plus $O(t)$, so after shrinking the collar it is a diffeomorphism and straightens the arc to $\{y_0\}\times[0,\epsilon)$. This is the same standard ball-arc collar as the radial endpoint collar of $a$. Thus the lifted upper arc is the original ball-arc tangle and the lower one is its image under $(x,t)\mapsto(x,-t)$, up to collar-supported isotopy. The boundary orientation traverses one lifted arc in the direction of $a$ and the other in the reverse direction. By [F2] and [F5], closing these two arcs with the fixed connected-sum gluing gives precisely the oriented type $K\#K^\dagger$. Therefore $\partial D$ has the required oriented knot type.

On $D$, the squared radial function is $\rho(s,t)=f(s)+t^2$. Its interior critical points are exactly $(s,0)$ where $f'(s)=0$. At each such point the Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(f''(s),2)$, which is nondegenerate and has index $0$ when $f''(s)>0$ and index $1$ when $f''(s)<0$ by [F7]. Thus there are no index-$2$ critical points, and step 4.1 identifies the boundary knot as $K\#K^\dagger$. This proves the statement.

citations.quote: An oriented circle is a smooth one-dimensional manifold diffeomorphic to the standard oriented circle. An abstract oriented cobordism from an oriented circle $C_0$ to an oriented circle $C_1$ is a compact oriented smooth surface $F$ together with orientation-preserving identifications of its incoming and outgoing boundary components such that $\partial F=-C_0\sqcup C_1$. Here $-C_0$ denotes the same circle with its orientation reversed. The cobordism is abstract: no embedding of $F$, $C_0$, or $C_1$ into a common three- or four-manifold is included in the data.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when a knot's Seifert pairing is formed. An integral Seifert lattice is a pair $(H,V)$ in which $H$ is a free abelian group of rank $2g$ for some $g\geq0$, and $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ is bilinear with $V-V^T$ unimodular. The rank-zero lattice is allowed, with the determinant of its empty skew matrix equal to $1$. A metabolizer is a primitive direct summand $M\subset H$ of rank $g$ such that $V(x,y)=0$ for every $x,y\in M$; the lattice is metabolic when it has a metabolizer. A chosen Seifert surface of an oriented knot gives such a lattice through the positive-push pairing. Its form is algebraically slice when that lattice is metabolic.

An isomorphism of integral Seifert lattices $(H,V)$ and $(H',V')$ is an integral group isomorphism $P:H\to H'$ satisfying $V'(Px,Py)=V(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in H$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the commutative monoid of these isomorphism classes under orthogonal direct sum, where $(H,V)\oplus(H',V')$ has underlying group $H\oplus H'$ and pairing $V\oplus V'$, with the rank-zero lattice as identity. The integral algebraic concordance group $G_{\mathbb Z}$ is the abelian group generated by symbols $[V]$ for $[V]\in\mathcal S$, subject to $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$ and $[M]=0$ for every metabolic lattice $M$. Two selected Seifert forms are algebraically concordant when they represent the same element of $G_{\mathbb Z}$. This form relation does not assert the existence of a smooth or locally flat topological concordance annulus between the knots.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in the unit four-ball $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ if and only if it is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $D\subset B^4$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk with oriented boundary $K$. Then the positive-push Seifert lattice $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is metabolic: it has a rank-$g$ primitive direct summand on which $V$ vanishes identically.

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$ with boundary an oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected oriented Seifert surface for $K$. After matching product collars and pushing the interior of $F$ slightly into $B^4$, the closed locally flat surface $\Sigma=F\cup_KD$ bounds a compact connected oriented locally flat three-manifold $R\subset B^4$. The conclusion includes an oriented ambient product neighborhood of $R$ on both sides, with the positive normal push-off along the $F$ portion of $\partial R=\Sigma$ lying on the complementary side of $R$.

Take the abstract annulus $S^1\times[0,1]$ and identify its lower and upper boundary circles orientation-preservingly with $C_0$ and $C_1$, orienting the annulus so its boundary is $-C_0\sqcup C_1$. For the fixed trefoil matrix in [F3], $$V+V^T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}.$$ Its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2+4\lambda+3=(\lambda+1)(\lambda+3)$, so its eigenvalues are $-1,-3$ and its signature is $-2$. More directly, for $x=(a,b)\ne0$ over $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$,
$$x^T(V+V^T)x=-2(a^2-ab+b^2)=-(a-b)^2-a^2-b^2<0.$$
Consequently $V$ cannot have a rank-one metabolizer: a nonzero vector in one would have zero value by [F5]. This is a calculation for the displayed Seifert surface and basis; no knot-level signature invariance is being inferred. The unknot's rank-zero form in [F4] still has signature zero.

If $U$ were smoothly concordant to $T$, reverse the interval coordinate to obtain smooth concordance of $T$ to the unknot. By [F6] and [A2], $T$ would bound a smooth proper disk. Apply the proved smooth branch [F7] to the particular trefoil Seifert surface in [F3]. It gives a rank-one metabolizer for $V$, contradicting the strict negative-definiteness calculation and [F5] in step 2.1. Thus the displayed abstract oriented annulus has no realization as a smooth concordance between its specified endpoint knots, refuting the claimed universal realization. derivations.claim: Choose a $\mathbb Q$-basis $v_1,\ldots,v_g$ of $L$. Clearing the finitely many denominators in the coordinates of each $v_i$ gives nonzero integer multiples $x_i\in H\cap L$. The $x_i$ remain $\mathbb Q$-linearly independent, so $M=H\cap L$ has rank at least $g$; it has rank at most $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=g$. Hence $\operatorname{rank}M=g$.
If $n\ne0$, $x\in H$, and $nx\in M$, then $nx\in L$ and therefore $x=n^{-1}(nx)\in L$ because $L$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace. Thus $x\in M$, so $M$ is saturated in $H$.

We prove by induction on $r$ that every saturated subgroup $P\subset\mathbb Z^r$ is a direct summand. The cases $P=0$ and $P=\mathbb Z^r$ are immediate. Otherwise choose a nonzero $p\in P$, divide its coordinates by their greatest common divisor, and use saturation to see that the resulting primitive vector $e_1$ still lies in $P$. The Euclidean algorithm gives a unimodular change of basis carrying $e_1$ to the first standard basis vector, so write $\mathbb Z^r=\mathbb Ze_1\oplus H'$. Every $p'\in P$ has a unique form $ae_1+h'$ with $h'\in H'$, and $h'=p'-ae_1\in P\cap H'$. Therefore $P=\mathbb Ze_1\oplus(P\cap H')$. The subgroup $P\cap H'$ is saturated in $H'$; its rank is $\operatorname{rank}P-1$, since the projection of $P$ to $\mathbb Ze_1$ is onto. Induction makes $P\cap H'$ a direct summand of $H'$, hence $P$ a direct summand of $\mathbb Z^r$.
Apply step 2.1 to the saturated rank-$g$ subgroup $M\subset H\cong\mathbb Z^{2g}$ from step 1.2. It is a direct summand of $H$.
Since $M\subset L$ and $V$ vanishes on $L\times L$, its restriction to $M\times M$ vanishes. Together with rank $g$ and the direct-summand conclusion of step 2.2, this proves the claim.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, and let $X_t$ be a smooth
time-dependent vector field on $M$ over $I$. For every $(s,p)\in I\times M$
there exist an open interval $J\subseteq I$ containing $s$, open
neighbourhoods $U_r$ of the evolving points, and a smooth map

$$ \Psi:\{(t,s,q): t,s\in J,\ q\in U_s\}\to M $$

such that $t\mapsto \Psi_{t,s}(q)$ is the unique solution of
$\dot\gamma(t)=X_t(\gamma(t))$ with $\Psi_{s,s}(q)=q$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to\mathbb R^k$ be continuous, where $M$ is a smooth manifold, and let $\varepsilon:M\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive continuous error function. Then there exists a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$\|\widetilde F(p)-F(p)\|<\varepsilon(p)\qquad\text{for all }p\in M.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be disjoint finite rational $1$-cycles in the boundary $S^3$ of the standard oriented $4$-ball $B^4$, each represented as a finite rational linear combination of oriented knots. Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ with $\partial P=\alpha$ and $\partial Q=\beta$, with common standard product collars at their respective boundaries and with their interiors in general position. Then the signed interior intersection number $P\cdot Q$ equals the bilinear extension of the linking number $\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ defined by positive meridians in $S^3$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

If $M$ is a compact topological manifold with boundary $A=\partial M$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $A$ and a homeomorphism
$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$
Consequently $A\hookrightarrow M$ is an unbased cofibration, and $M\setminus A\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. The manifold is Hausdorff and second countable by convention. All three conclusions require no AC.

derivations.claim: Use the given boundary product collar to extend $D$ a little beyond $S^3$. Its normal quotient planes are represented by smooth orthogonal projection matrices $Q$ in the ambient Euclidean space. Parametrize the original disk radially from one interior point. Along each radial segment solve $\dot U=[\dot Q,Q]U$ from one fixed oriented orthonormal frame. The skew-symmetric coefficient preserves norms, and compactness gives a bounded coefficient on the finite parameter disk and time interval, so the local solutions of [F2] extend over the entire interval and depend smoothly on the endpoint. This gives a smooth frame of the disk's normal quotient bundle. Choose an ambient metric product-shaped on the end collar, by a one-variable cutoff interpolation with its product metric. Its orthogonal normal bundle is isomorphic to the quotient and inherits the frame. Its geodesic map is the local flow of the smooth coordinate equation $\ddot x^k=-\tfrac12g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_jg_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij})\dot x^i\dot x^j$, whose transformation rule follows by the chain rule. At the zero section its derivative adds tangent and normal vectors, hence is invertible. Extend across the end collar and apply [F2] there. Compactness of the original disk gives a uniform injective tube radius: otherwise equal images of distinct normal vectors tending to zero have convergent basepoints, their limits are equal, and the local inverse at that zero vector is contradicted. Shrink also inside all local flow domains. This constructs an actual smooth disk tube $D^2\times D^2$, product-shaped at its boundary.

A small nonzero constant frame vector gives a disjoint proper parallel disk $D'$. By [F3], the linking of its boundary with $K$ equals $D\mathbin\cdot D'=0$. Hence the tube's induced boundary framing is precisely the preferred zero framing. Remove its interior and round the product corners to obtain the actual compact smooth disk exterior $X$. In the decomposition $B^4=X\cup(D^2\times D^2)$ the overlap retracts to $D^2\times S^1$. Since the ball and tube are contractible, integral Mayer–Vietoris gives $H_1(X)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ and $H_i(X)=0$ for $i>1$. Its marked boundary is the zero surgery $M(K)=E_K\cup_{T^2}(D^2\times S^1)$, with the disk meridian the zero longitude and the circle the positive meridian. The boundary meridian therefore induces an $H_1$ isomorphism to $X$.

We construct a boundary circle map with the actual prescribed fiber, rather than presuming that $K$ is fibered. Truncate $F$ at the knot tube to a proper surface in $E_K$, and cap its boundary with $D^2\times\{1\}$ in the inner solid torus. Call the resulting closed connected surface $\Sigma_0\subset M(K)$. Give a small normal product of $F$ the signed coordinate $u$ whose positive direction is the positive Seifert push, and put $f_0=\exp(2\pi i u)$ there. On the inner $D^2\times S^1$ put $f_0(x,z)=z$, matching these choices in the peripheral collar. Cut the rest of the knot exterior along that product of $F$. Its two faces have real phase values $\epsilon$ and $1-\epsilon$, and its remaining torus annulus has the ordinary lifted angular coordinate between them. These prescriptions agree in their product corner collars. Extend the real phase to the remaining compact cut manifold by finite smooth collar cutoffs and a partition of unity, with all values in $(0,1)$ and constant $1/2$ away from its prescribed boundary collars. Convexity keeps the extended values away from $0$ modulo $1$. Exponentiating gives a smooth map $f_0:M(K)\to S^1$ with $1$ as a regular value, fiber exactly $\Sigma_0$, and positive coorientation on the $F$ part. Its induced homomorphism on $H_1$ is the positive meridian map: crossing $F$ once positively increases the lifted phase by one, exactly the intersection convention in [F4].

The same meridian class on $X$ is represented by a continuous map $g:X\to S^1$. To construct it, use the finite CW model of [F3]: send a maximal tree to the basepoint, the remaining one-cells to loops of the stipulated integer degrees, fill each two-cell because its relator has degree zero, and fill higher cells because the universal cover $\mathbb R$ of the circle is contractible. Transport the map by the actual homotopy model. The boundary homomorphism of $g$ equals that of $f_0$ by step 2.1. Smooth $g$ by viewing it in $\mathbb R^2$, extending constantly across boundary collars to the smooth double, applying [F2] within error $1/4$ and projecting the result radially to $S^1$. Normalized straight-line interpolation preserves its homotopy class. The smooth boundary ratio $f_0/g$ has zero degree on every loop, so it has a global smooth real argument: lift its argument along paths from a fixed point; zero loop increments make it path-independent, and local arguments prove smoothness. First make $g$ constant in a smaller boundary collar by a smooth reparametrization of the collar depth. Multiplication there by the exponential of the lifted boundary argument times a cutoff changes $g$ to a smooth $f:X\to S^1$ equal to $f_0$ on that smaller entire collar.

Make $1$ a regular value in the remaining compact interior while keeping that collar fixed. Cover the compact critical set on the fiber by finitely many interior charts with bumps positive on smaller cores. For small parameters $a_j$, the family $f_a=f\exp(2\pi i\sum_j a_j\phi_j)$ has derivative spanning the circle tangent in some parameter direction at each such core. Off these cores the original fiber map is already transverse, and sufficiently small parameters preserve that property by compactness and the inverse-function local rank criterion. Thus the total family is transverse to $1$. Parametric transversality [F2] supplies an arbitrarily small parameter with transverse slice. It is unchanged on the retained boundary collar. Its inverse image $R_0$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with product boundary $\partial R_0=\Sigma_0$; orient it with the normal-last product convention so that its boundary has the stated orientation of $\Sigma_0$. Since $\Sigma_0$ is connected, exactly one component of $R_0$ meets it; discard all closed components.

On the inner tube boundary the fiber is exactly $D^2\times\{1\}$ and is product-shaped in its normal collar, so attach the radial product $D^2\times[0,r]$ down that fixed angle to the zero section $D$. At the common peripheral circle it joins the original $F$ collar; their quadrant coordinates agree with the zero-longitude marking in step 2.1. Round these product sectors. The result is a compact connected smooth embedded $R$ with boundary the rounded capped surface $F\cup_K(-D)$, with $F$ carrying its original orientation. Here, as in the Statement's collar adjustment, use a small collar embedding of the ball into its interior and the corresponding rounding to regard the capped closed surface and its spanning $R$ as interior representatives. This retains their identification with $F\cup_KD$ and all old $F$ homology curves; it does not leave an interior point of a closed capped surface on the outer boundary. The normal coorientation of $R_0$ on $F$ was the positive Seifert direction in step 3.1, so after the same collar transport the positive push-off lies on that complementary side of $R$.

Finally the orientations of $R$ and of the four-ball supply a continuous unit smooth normal field on $R$. Extend it in finitely many coordinate neighborhoods by smooth cutoffs to an ambient smooth vector field. Along its small-time flow, the derivative in the normal/time direction together with the tangent directions is invertible at time zero. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ bounds a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ whose oriented boundary is $K$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact oriented smooth $1$-manifold and give $\partial W$ the outward-normal-first orientation ([[def-induced-boundary-orientation]]). The boundary is a finite $0$-manifold, so its orientation at a boundary point $p$ is a sign $\varepsilon(p)\in\{+1,-1\}$; then $$\sum_{p\in\partial W}\varepsilon(p)=0.$$ On each closed-interval component the two boundary points carry opposite signs; circle components contribute nothing. With the standard orientation of $[a,b]$ the outward-normal-first convention gives $\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}$.

If $X$ is a nonempty contractible topological space, then for every $n\geq 0$
and every abelian group $G$,
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\cong H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(\ast;G),$$
where $\ast$ denotes a one-point space.

Let $X$ be a compact oriented smooth $x$-manifold without boundary, let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $Z\subseteq M$ be a closed oriented embedded $z$-submanifold with $x+z=n$ ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]). For a smooth $f:X\to M$ transverse to $Z$, the **oriented intersection number** is the finite sum

$$I(f,Z):=\sum_{p\in f^{-1}(Z)}\varepsilon(p)\in\mathbb Z,$$

with the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]]; the sum is finite by [[lem-compact-transverse-complementary-intersections-are-finite]]. For an arbitrary smooth $g:X\to M$, choose a transverse $f$ homotopic to $g$ ([[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], under Countable Choice; the homotopy is a smooth family in the sense of [[def-smooth-family-of-maps-and-evaluation-map]]) and set $I(g,Z):=I(f,Z)$; independence of the choice is [[thm-oriented-intersection-number-is-homotopy-invariant]], not assumed here. For compact oriented complementary-dimensional submanifolds $A,B\subseteq M$, where one is compact and the other closed, one sets $I(A,B):=I(i_A,B)$ with $i_A$ the inclusion, so the first factor is the submanifold $A$. If the source is not compact, or the target submanifold is not closed, the sum may fail to be finite or invariant; the safe extension by properness with compact trace is recorded in the remark on properness later on this page. Countable Choice is assumed for selecting transverse representatives and for the classification used to prove independence of that selection; the signs, the finite sum and the empty case (which contributes $0$) are choice-free.

For transverse maps $f:X^x\to M$, $g:Z^z\to M$ with compact oriented boundaryless sources and $x+z=\dim M$, define $I(f,g)$ as the sum of the local signs of [[def-local-oriented-intersection-sign]] over $X\times_MZ$. This set is closed in the compact product because $M$ is Hausdorff, and discrete by [[def-transverse-complementary-dimensional-intersection-set]], so the sum is finite. If $g$ is an inclusion this recovers $I(f,Z)$. Ambient compactness is unnecessary in either construction.

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold and let $f:X^x\to M$ and $g:Z^z\to M$ be smooth maps from oriented smooth manifolds, with $x+z=n$ and $f,g$ transverse in the sense of [[def-transverse-smooth-maps]]. Let $a\in X$, $b\in Z$ satisfy $f(a)=g(b)=y$. Then $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ and $T_yM$ have the same dimension, and transversality says that

$$(df_a,dg_b):T_aX\oplus T_bZ\longrightarrow T_yM,\qquad (v,w)\mapsto df_a(v)+dg_b(w),$$

is surjective, hence a linear isomorphism ([[def-transverse-linear-subspaces]]); the sum is direct because the dimensions add up. The ordered direct sum $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ carries the product orientation with the first factor $T_aX$ and the second factor $T_bZ$ ([[def-product-orientation]]), and the three tangent spaces carry their manifold orientations ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]).

The **local oriented intersection sign** $\varepsilon(a,b)\in\{+1,-1\}$ is $+1$ when this isomorphism carries the product orientation of $T_aX\oplus T_bZ$ to the orientation of $T_yM$, and $-1$ otherwise; equivalently it is the orientation sign of the induced isomorphism of determinant lines ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]], [[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

For transverse oriented embedded submanifolds $A^a,B^b\subseteq M$ with $a+b=n$ one takes $f$ and $g$ to be the inclusion maps ([[def-transverse-embedded-submanifolds]]); the sign at $p\in A\cap B$ then compares $T_pA\oplus T_pB\to T_pM$ with $A$ first. The empty intersection is allowed and carries no signs. In dimension zero the sign compares the two orientation rays directly, and for $x=z=n=0$ it is $\varepsilon_X(a)\varepsilon_Z(b)\varepsilon_M(y)$, the product of the two source point signs and the ambient point sign. The factor order is part of the definition: with the two factors exchanged the signs are multiplied by $(-1)^{ab}$, exactly the graded-commutativity sign measured later on this page by the factor-interchange theorem. No compactness, closedness hypothesis or choice axiom is used in this local definition.

For an oriented manifold with boundary, orient $T_p\partial M$ by the **outward-normal-first** rule: an outward vector first, followed by a positive boundary determinant, is a positive determinant of $T_pM$.

For oriented vector spaces use the ordered determinant isomorphism $\det(V\oplus W)\cong\det V\otimes\det W$ and take the tensor product of the selected rays. Fibrewise this defines the product orientation.

derivations.claim: First consider disjoint oriented knots $\alpha,\beta$ and two admissible choices $P,P'$ bounding $\alpha$ with the same product collar, while $Q$ is fixed. Their difference $C=P-P'$ is a closed rational $2$-cycle supported in the interior of $B^4$, because the common boundary collars cancel. By [F3], $C=\partial Z$ for a finite rational $3$-chain $Z$ supported in the interior. Put $Z$ and $Q$ in general position relative to their boundary collars. The transverse intersection $Z\cap Q$ is a compact oriented $1$-chain. The product-orientation convention in [F4] makes its boundary count equal to the intersection count $(P-P')\cdot Q$ plus the term from $Z\cap\partial Q$; the latter is empty because $Z$ lies in the interior and $\partial Q=\beta\subset S^3$. By [F2], its signed boundary count is zero, so $P\cdot Q=P'\cdot Q$. The same argument with $Q-Q'$ shows independence of the second bounding chain. Bilinearity gives this independence for finite rational combinations of knots.

By [F5], choose an oriented Seifert surface $S_\beta\subset S^3$ for each knot component of $\beta$, and similarly choose a cap for each component of $\alpha$. It suffices by bilinearity to consider one knot component of each. Choose a collar depth $0<\epsilon$ in $B^4$. Make $Q$ a graph of $S_\beta$ in the boundary collar with depth zero on $\beta$ and strictly between $0$ and $\epsilon/2$ on its interior. Make $P$ consist of the product collar $\alpha\times[0,\epsilon]$ followed by a cap at depth $\epsilon$. Then $P$ and $Q$ intersect exactly above $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. At each such point, the oriented tangent basis of the collar of $P$ is $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a)$, where $a$ is the positive tangent to $\alpha$ and $n_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outward normal of $B^4$; the tangent basis of $Q$ is a positive basis $(s_1,s_2)$ of $S_\beta$, up to radial components which do not change the determinant. By [F4], $(n_{\mathrm{out}},a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive exactly when $(a,s_1,s_2)$ is positive in the boundary orientation. Thus the $4$-dimensional intersection sign is exactly the $3$-dimensional sign of $\alpha\cap S_\beta$. Hence $P\cdot Q=\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ by [F1].

Step 1.1 shows the intersection number is independent of admissible collared bounding chains, and step 1.2 computes it for one convenient choice. Hence the equality holds for all such $P,Q$ when the boundaries are knots. Expanding finite rational cycles into their oriented knot components and using bilinearity of both signed intersection and linking proves the stated equality.

Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ with $\partial P=\alpha$ and $\partial Q=\beta$, with common standard product collars at their respective boundaries and with their interiors in general position. Then the signed interior intersection number $P\cdot Q$ equals the bilinear extension of the linking number $\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ defined by positive meridians in $S^3$.

Let $H$ be a free abelian group of rank $2g$ and let $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ be a bilinear form. Write $H_{\mathbb Q}=H\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and extend $V$ $\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to $H_{\mathbb Q}$. If $L\subset H_{\mathbb Q}$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace of dimension $g$ and $V(x,y)=0$ for all $x,y\in L$, then $M=H\cap L$ is a rank-$g$ direct summand of $H$ and $V|_{M\times M}=0$.

$$H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H_k^{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$$
in every integer degree. This isomorphism is natural for smooth maps. The proof smooths only finitely many simplices at a time. For boundary targets it moves a finite compact set into the interior; it does not prescribe arbitrary boundary faces during smoothing.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

If $M$ is a compact topological manifold with boundary $A=\partial M$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $A$ and a homeomorphism
$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$
Consequently $A\hookrightarrow M$ is an unbased cofibration, and $M\setminus A\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. The manifold is Hausdorff and second countable by convention. All three conclusions require no AC.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.
For a finite CW complex, $\chi(X)=\sum_n(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

derivations.claim: First assume the given disk is smooth. Construct $R$ by [F5], and write $\Sigma=\partial R=F\cup D$ after matching collars. The Axiom of Choice [A1] is the hypothesis under which the supplied Seifert-pairing and duality interfaces are invoked. Capping the sole boundary circle of $F$ by a disk does not change $H_1$ because that circle is already the boundary of the oriented fundamental $2$-chain of $F$; by [F9] and exactness [F10], $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $2g$. In the pair sequence [F10], $H_0(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_0(R;\mathbb Q)$ is an isomorphism because both are connected. Exactness therefore makes $H_1(R;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ surjective. By [F2] and [F14], the target has dimension $b_2(R)$, so the image of $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $b_1(R)-b_2(R)$.

Let $\widehat R$ be the double of $R$ along $\Sigma$, with the second copy oppositely oriented so the orientations glue. Its two copies have open collar thickenings with intersection retracting to $\Sigma$, so [F11] gives $\chi(\widehat R)=2\chi(R)-\chi(\Sigma)$. By [F12] and [F13], $\chi(\widehat R)=0$, and by [F9], $\chi(\Sigma)=2-2g$; hence $\chi(R)=1-g$. Also [F2] gives $H_3(R;\mathbb Q)\cong H^0(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)=0$: a relative zero-cocycle is locally constant on the connected $R$ and vanishes on the nonempty connected $\Sigma$, so it is zero. With $b_0(R)=1$, the rational Euler-characteristic identity [F13] implies $b_1(R)-b_2(R)=g$. Thus the kernel $L=\ker(H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q))$, identified with a subspace of $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, has dimension $2g-g=g$.

Let $x,y\in L$, represented by finite rational smooth cycles on $F$ away from $K$. Their rational bounding chains in $R$ can be taken smooth. Indeed [F6] first supplies finite smooth real bounding chains; their boundary equations are one finite rational linear system on the real coefficients of finitely many smooth simplices, so rational Gaussian elimination supplies rational coefficients solving the same equations. Use the pre-collar-push model in [F5] to place the boundary cycles back on the actual $F\subset S^3$. A finite intrinsic collar push moves the interiors of their bounding chains off the boundary of $R$, fixing the prescribed boundary collars, so the chains miss the product corner $K$. The model is smooth on a neighborhood of these compact supports. Its positive normal field is tangent to $S^3$ along $F$ and points in the positive Seifert direction; extend it by finitely many bumps to an ambient field tangent to $S^3$ there. Its small-time flow pushes the first bounding chain $X$ off $R$, with boundary exactly $x^+$ in $S^3$, while the second chain $Y$ stays in $R$ with boundary $y$. Compactness and the product neighborhood keep the two supports disjoint. Their common standard end collars and empty intersection make them admissible for [F3], so $\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)=X^+\mathbin\cdot Y=0$. By [F1] this is $V_{\mathbb Q}(x,y)$. Hence $L$ is a rational Seifert-isotropic subspace.

By [F4], $M=H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\cap L$ is a rank-$g$ direct summand and $V|_{M\times M}=0$. By [F8], $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is an integral Seifert lattice; the metabolic-form definition therefore makes $M$ a metabolizer. This proves the entire metabolic conclusion whenever the supplied slice disk is smooth.

For the arbitrary locally flat disk use the TOP $R$ and its actual product from [F5]. The duality and pair-sequence computation of steps 1.1–1.2 applies to this compact oriented TOP three-manifold: [F7] supplies finite homology and [F13] gives its Euler-characteristic formula, [F2] applies in the TOP category, and [F11]–[F12] give the double's Euler characteristic. By [F9], $\chi(\Sigma)=2-2g$ and $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $2g$. Thus, without putting a smooth structure on the embedding, the rational kernel $L=\ker(H_1(F;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q))$ has dimension $g$.

Represent $x,y\in L$ by finite rational smooth cycles in the given $F$, away from $K$, and choose finite rational CONTINUOUS bounding chains in $R$. Use its pre-collar-push model and the actual positive normal product of [F5]. Push the first chain into the positive complementary side, with boundary the actual positive Seifert push $x^+$; leave the second chain in $R$ with boundary $y$. An intrinsic boundary-collar push of their interiors and the common product near $F$ give the usual collared bounding chains in $B^4$, missing the corner $K$. Their supports are disjoint compact sets by the actual two-sided product. Choose disjoint relatively open smooth ambient neighborhoods $U,V\subset B^4$ of those supports, including their boundary cycles; these are smooth manifolds with boundary as open subsets of the standard smooth ball. In $U$, [F6] makes the smooth cycle $x^+$ bound a finite smooth real chain, since it bounds continuously there; likewise $y$ bounds in $V$. In each finite set of occurring simplices the equations for the boundary coefficients are rational, so rational Gaussian elimination replaces the real coefficients by rational ones without enlarging support. Near $S^3$, move the interiors inward and attach the standard product of the fixed boundary cycle with the collar interval. This puts both chains in common standard end collars, still in disjoint $U,V$. They therefore have empty interior intersection, and [F3] gives $V_{\mathbb Q}(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)=0$. The smoothing here concerns only chains in the disjoint SMOOTH ambient regions; it assumes no smooth structure on $R$ or its TOP normal chart.

Apply the unchanged integral-saturation result [F4] to this $g$-dimensional rational isotropic subspace: $M=H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\cap L$ is a primitive rank-$g$ direct summand with $V|_{M\times M}=0$. By [F8] the pairing is on an integral Seifert lattice, so the metabolic-form definition makes $M$ a metabolizer. This proves the full locally flat Statement, with the external geometric inputs explicitly located in [F5]'s hypersurface supplier and the resolved smooth/rank/saturation arguments retained.
